The client controls this value: a cursor string such as '1:-5:0' parses to a negative offset via Cursor.from_string. The additional consequences and base-path observation do not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result nearly verbatim

The new class copies most of BasePaginator.get_result (cursor handling, hits counting, prev-row trimming, build_cursor call) and adds only a negative-offset branch that is broken (see the line 882 finding). Any future fix to the base logic will silently diverge in this copy. The class also duplicates get_item_key and value_from_cursor, which are already identical to DateTimePaginator's behavior for the sort keys used here. The change should either extend BasePaginator with a flag or be reverted.

Experimental pagination path is gated by a client query parameter and an admin-only flag

The optimized paginator is selected by the client-supplied query parameter optimized_pagination=true, and it enables advanced features for superusers and users with global access. This ships an unreviewed, experimental code path (negative offset handling that the code comments describe as allowing 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds') to production behind a user-controlled switch. The comment claiming permissions are enforced at the queryset level is not backed by any check in the code. Access checks should be explicit and tested, or the path should not be exposed.

Deploy will break in-flight segments stored as Redis sets

process_spans now uses ZADD on span-buf:s:* keys, and add-buffer.lua switched from SCARD/SUNIONSTORE to ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE. Any span-buf:s:* key written by the previous code is a Redis set, so ZADD, ZCARD and ZUNIONSTORE on it fail with WRONGTYPE, and _load_segment_data's ZSCAN fails as well. Segments buffered before the deploy (up to span_buffer_timeout / root timeout, and the queue entries still reference them) will error during processing and flushing. No key migration, dual-read, or key renaming is included.

Span eviction silently discards data with no log or metric

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin removes the lowest-scored (oldest) spans from the set. Those spans are dropped without any counter, log, or metric. The previous Python-side guard (max_segment_spans) did emit metrics and an error log, and that check has now been removed from _load_segment_data. Operators have no way to see that segments are being truncated.

ZUNIONSTORE sums scores for duplicate payloads

ZUNIONSTORE uses the default SUM aggregate. When the same span payload is present in both the source and destination sets (for example, a redelivered Kafka message), its score is doubled, so its end_timestamp_precise no longer reflects the span's real end time. This distorts the eviction order introduced by this PR (zpopmin evicts by score) and any ordering that depends on it. An explicit AGGREGATE MIN or MAX should be used, or duplicates should be otherwise handled.

Redirect loop limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without updating dependent behavior

The redirect-walk loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000 and the explanatory comment about deep segment trees was removed. Trees with a redirect depth above 1000 will now be silently left unjoined, where previously they were joined. This is a behavior change that is not mentioned in the PR and has no test covering depth above 1000.

max_segment_spans is now a dead parameter

The max_segment_spans check was removed from _load_segment_data, but SpansBuffer.__init__ still accepts and stores max_segment_spans (default 1001). Nothing reads it, so the configuration is misleading: callers believe they can tune a span-count limit that no longer does anything. The Lua limit of 1000 is now the only span cap and is hardcoded.

Hard KeyError on messages lacking end_timestamp_precise

process_batch now reads val["end_timestamp_precise"] directly. Any span message without that field (for example from an older Relay or a schema gap) raises KeyError and fails the whole batch in the consumer, rather than being handled or defaulted. The rest of the code already uses .get() for optional fields such as parent_span_id and is_remote.

No tests for the new eviction, the 1000-span cap, or the optimized paginator

The PR adds spans-per-segment eviction via zpopmin and a new OptimizedCursorPaginator with negative-offset handling, but no tests cover either. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans and checks which survive, no test for duplicate payload score aggregation, and no test for negative or is_prev cursor offsets in pagination. The existing negative-offset bug would have been caught by a single test.

false_positives.candidate:
Allowlist eligibility is cached for 60s and the invalidation helper is never called

The eligibility result is cached under a key derived only from organization id and project ids, with a 60 second TTL. Changes to `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` are therefore not visible for up to a minute. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` (lines 67-74) exists for this purpose but nothing in the PR calls it, so it is dead code and the stale window cannot be cleared on allowlist changes. The docstring calls eventual consistency acceptable, but the allowlist is a rollout control, so a removed project can keep getting upsampled counts for a minute.

Cache key built from Python hash() of the project id tuple

The cache key embeds `hash(tuple(sorted(...)))` instead of the ids themselves. Distinct project sets can collide to the same key, which would return an eligibility answer computed for a different set of projects. Using the sorted id list (or a stable digest) in the key avoids this. The same expression is duplicated at line 73.

Membership test is O(n*m) against a list allowlist

`project_id in allowlist` runs against a list for each project, so the check is O(projects * allowlist size) and is repeated on every request. Converting the allowlist to a set once would be cheaper. This is minor unless the allowlist grows.

Comments claim caching and late optimization that the code does not implement

The comments say the eligibility check is a 'cached result' that 'ensures consistent behavior' and that the decision is stored 'to apply later ... allows for better query optimization and caching'. The code just calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` and copies the boolean into `upsampling_enabled`. The transform is then applied in up to three places, each recomputing from `query_columns`. The comments mislead maintainers about what is cached and why, and the duplicated transform blocks should be collapsed into one.

Unrelated change to a public error message

The topEvents validation message changed from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This is not part of the upsampling feature. Clients or tests matching the old string will break, and the change should be split out or justified.

upsampled_count is only defined on the discover function converter

`transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling` rewrites `count()` to `upsampled_count() as count`, and that rewrite is applied whenever the dataset is `errors` (`_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` returns True for it). The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is added only to the discover dataset's function converter. Unless the errors dataset shares this converter, queries on the errors dataset will fail with an unknown function error. The PR's tests only cover the discover path through the endpoint, so this is not caught.

upsampled_count ignores the alias set by the caller and hard-codes sum(sample_weight)

The function returns `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` with no guard for events lacking `sample_weight`. The comment says the schema guarantees this, but the transform is driven purely by project allowlist membership. An allowlisted project with events that have no sample_weight will silently produce 0 counts for those events, and nothing in the query path validates this assumption.

Helper swallows all exceptions and is applied to every stored test event

`_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling` wraps its lookups and conversions in bare `except Exception: pass`. Failures are silently ignored, which makes test data problems hard to diagnose. It also runs for every event in `store_event`, so any test that stores an event with an `error_sampling` context now gets a `sample_rate` set implicitly. That side effect is not documented and is not limited to the upsampling tests.

Stray submodule pointer committed to the repository

The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing a submodule commit hash. It is unrelated to error upsampling and looks like an accidental commit. The PR description 'Test 3' also gives reviewers no context. Both should be removed or explained before merge.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key concatenates unescaped fields, so distinct requests can collide

userPermDenialCacheKey joins userUID, action, name and parent with '_' and no escaping. Different tuples produce the same key: name "a_b" with empty parent and name "a" with parent "b" both yield "...._a_b_" / "...._a_b"-style collisions. The key also shares the "perm_" prefix with userPermCacheKey. A collision makes a denial for one resource apply to another, so an unrelated resource is wrongly denied until the TTL expires. Use a separator that cannot appear in the fields (or a hash of a structured tuple).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: underscore-delimited, unescaped concatenation in userPermDenialCacheKey can produce collisions between distinct field tuples, causing incorrect denial cache hits and permission denials. The additional prefix concern and imprecise example do not change the core match.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache short-circuits before the DB fallback, so a cached denial can keep hiding a newly granted permission

The denial cache is checked first in Check and returns deny immediately, before the cached-permission lookup and the DB fallback that this PR adds. A denial is written with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) whenever the DB result is not allowed. If a user is checked on a resource before its permission row exists (for example, a dashboard or folder just created by that user, or a frontend poll), the denial is cached for 30s. Once the permission is written, every Check for that same user/action/name/folder returns false until the entry expires, which is the exact symptom this PR is meant to fix. The denial entry should be bypassed or invalidated when the permission is granted, or the check should go to the DB before trusting a denial. At minimum this trade-off needs to be documented and covered by a test.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

For such an ACTIVE integration the check raises KeyError and the setup request returns a 500 instead of the intended error page. Use a safe lookup and fail closed with the error response.

GitHub user verification is skipped entirely for installations without an existing Integration

When no Integration row exists for the installation_id, the code returns `pipeline.next_step()` immediately. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock

The function reads the cache under RLock, releases it, and then takes the write Lock unconditionally. If several requests arrive while the cache is still nil, or while a dev-mode request is in flight, each one passes the first check and then rebuilds the manifest from disk (and possibly the CDN) in turn. Once a goroutine holds the write lock, it should re-check entryPointAssetsCache (for non-dev) and return it if another goroutine has already populated it. Without that, the lock only serializes the work and does not avoid the duplicate loads.

The sync path returns the `fetch` Response, but the non-sync path returns the value of `refreshFunction()`, which callers expect in provider-specific shapes (e.g. Google reads `res.data`, Zoho reads `tokenInfo.data.error`, HubSpot reads `expiresIn`). With sync enabled, Google's `res?.data` is undefined, so `token.access_token` throws. That error is swallowed by the catch, and the stale token is returned silently. Zoho Bigin's `tokenInfo.data.error` throws an uncaught TypeError in `refreshAccessToken`, breaking event creation. The sync response is also never checked for `response.ok`, so an error from the sync endpoint is handled as if it were a successful token refresh.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistent return-shape bug: the sync branch returns a raw fetch Response without .data, causing Google's res?.data to be undefined and token.access_token to throw. Its additional observations do not change the core match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Salesforce now refreshes its token on every client construction, bypassing the sync endpoint

`getClient` unconditionally POSTs to login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token and writes the result to the DB, for every user and every service instantiation. It does not go through `refreshOAuthTokens`, so self-hosters with `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` never get their sync endpoint used for Salesforce, and non-sync installs gain an extra network round trip and a DB write each time. Its `statusText !== "OK"` check is also brittle, since HTTP/2 responses may have an empty statusText.
true_positives.reasoning: Although the candidate primarily discusses unconditional refreshes and bypassing the sync endpoint, it explicitly identifies the same brittle statusText check: successful responses can have an empty statusText and therefore be misclassified. This matches the golden issue of checking statusText instead of response.ok.

false_positives.candidate:
`prisma` is used but never imported in the Salesforce calendar service

`getClient` now calls `prisma.credential.update(...)`, but the file's import list has no `prisma` import (only jsforce, rrule, zod, CalEventParser, constants, http-error, logger, types, getAppKeysFromSlug, parseRefreshTokenResponse). This is a ReferenceError at runtime and a type error at build time, so every Salesforce calendar operation fails.

Expiry computed from `expires_in` becomes NaN when sync mode omits that field

After switching to `parseRefreshTokenResponse`, in sync mode the parsed data may not contain `expires_in`. `Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000` is then NaN. The stored `expiry_date` becomes NaN, and `isTokenValid` (`(expires_in || expiry_date) < Date.now()`) evaluates false, so the adapter never refreshes the token again.

Decrypted keys are unvalidated and JSON.parse can throw an unhandled error

`JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` is not wrapped in try/catch, so a wrong key or malformed payload produces an unstructured 500. The parsed value is then written directly to `credential.key` with no per-app schema check, so any JSON shape is stored and can break the app's CalendarService when it later parses the credential.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`

The shared secret from the request header is compared with `!==` against the env value. This is a timing-sensitive comparison for an authentication secret; `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers should be used. The header lookup also depends on the configured header name being lowercase, which Node enforces for incoming headers.

New webhook endpoint and token-refresh changes have no tests

The PR adds an authenticated endpoint that writes credentials, plus new refresh logic in parseRefreshTokenResponse and refreshOAuthTokens that branches on env vars and userId. The checklist confirms no tests were added. The bugs above (placeholder refresh token, NaN expiry, the broken schema) would be caught by unit tests on these helpers.

Moved OAuth utilities may leave other importers of the old paths broken

encodeOAuthState, decodeOAuthState and createOAuthAppCredential were moved to `_utils/oauth/`. Only the listed app files were updated. If other apps or shared code still import `_utils/encodeOAuthState`, `_utils/decodeOAuthState` or `_utils/createOAuthAppCredential`, they will fail at build time. The diff does not show a full repository search.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code can be replayed by concurrent logins (read-modify-write race)

The backup code is consumed by decrypting the list, nulling the entry, and writing the whole list back with a plain `prisma.user.update`. There is no transaction, row lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent login requests that submit the same valid code can both read the unused list, both pass the `indexOf` check, and both succeed. This defeats the single-use guarantee. Consuming the code should be atomic, for example by re-reading inside a transaction with a version check or using a conditional update on the stored value.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same read-modify-write race: concurrent login requests can validate the same unused backup code before either update is persisted, allowing it to be accepted more than once and violating one-time-use semantics.

false_positives.candidate:
Lark createEvent always uses the first destination calendar, so multi-host collective events are not created per host

Lark's createEvent, createAttendees, updateEvent and deleteEvent all take `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar` and ignore which credential is calling. CalendarManager calls each credential's createEvent with the full destination array. In a collective event with two hosts, every host's Lark credential therefore writes to host #1's calendar, and host #2's calendar gets no event. The same pattern applies to Office365 (createEvent, line 73 of that file) and CalDAV (createEvent filter in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts). The PR's stated goal of letting each host receive the event is not met for these integrations.

The destination externalId is attached to the result but never passed to the calendar services

createEvent now receives `externalId` and calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`, dropping the externalId. Only the Google service uses the credential to pick a calendar. Other services read event.destinationCalendar[0] or filter by it, so the per-destination externalId is lost. EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents (line 370) passes `destination.externalId` into createEvent, which is then discarded, so each destination entry results in the same write. The result's `externalId` field is also set from an argument that does nothing for these integrations, so the references stored for the booking will not match the calendars actually written to.

Team destination calendars are silently dropped when the organizer has no destination calendar

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar. The following line does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`, which is a no-op on null. For a collective event where the organizer has no destination but other hosts do, the other hosts' calendars are never used, which is the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix. The array should be initialised rather than optionally pushed to.

Team destination calendars can be duplicated and are collected inside a parallel map

teamDestinationCalendars is pushed inside `users.slice(1).map(async ...)`. The push happens before the await in each callback, so ordering is nondeterministic. Also, if multiple hosts share a destination calendar or an existing entry is already in evt.destinationCalendar, duplicates are not removed, so createAllCalendarEvents will write the same event more than once. Collecting the calendars synchronously after the users list is built, then de-duplicating by id, would avoid both problems.

With two calendar references (the multi-host case this PR enables), each booking's event is deleted twice or more, and the duplicate deleteEvent calls push extra promises into apiDeletes. The recurring deletion should run once, outside the per-reference loop.

Office365 createEvent ignores the credential and writes every destination to the first calendar

createEvent reads `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []` and uses that calendar's externalId for the URL. With multiple destinations, each per-destination createEvent call writes an event to the first calendar rather than the one belonging to its credential. This creates duplicate events on one account and none on the others.

No tests added for the multi-host collective behaviour being fixed

The PR adds a new multi-destination code path in EventManager, CalendarManager and the booking handlers, but the checklist says no tests were added and the testing section relies on manual Loom recordings. Given how many call sites changed from a single destination to an array, unit tests for EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents and updateAllCalendarEvents with multiple destinations would be needed to catch the regressions above.

Callers that index the store without `await` (any call site not updated in this PR) now receive a Promise, so `"lib" in app` is false and the code silently treats the app as not implemented, e.g. `getCalendar` logs a 'not implemented' warning and returns null.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

As a result the calendar deletions are fire-and-forget: the handler reports success before they complete, and any rejection (e.g. from `deleteEvent`) becomes an unhandled rejection rather than an error surfaced to the caller. Use `for...of` with `await` or `Promise.all` over mapped promises, as the non-recurring branch already does.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same async forEach bug: callback promises are not awaited, causing fire-and-forget deletions, premature completion, and unhandled rejections. It also recommends the same fixes, for...of with await or Promise.all over mapped promises.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() permanently shuts down the shared queue pool

`SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` (and `join()`, which calls it) calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. In `ResultsStrategyFactory.create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, the same `self.queue_pool` is passed to every strategy the factory creates. StreamProcessor creates a new strategy on each partition assignment and closes the old one on rebalance. The first close therefore shuts down all queues and workers for the factory. Every later `create_with_partitions` returns a strategy whose `submit` puts into a shut-down queue, so messages fail or are never processed. Pool lifetime should be owned by the factory, not by an individual strategy.

Kafka commit function is invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs on its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes arroyo's `commit` callback. Arroyo's consumer is not thread-safe and expects commits to happen on the StreamProcessor thread that also polls. Calling commit from this thread can race with poll/assign/close on the same KafkaConsumer, and can produce undefined behaviour or errors during rebalances. Commits should be requested from the main processing thread, for example in `poll()` or `submit()`.

A missing offset permanently stalls commits for the partition

In `get_committable_offsets`, the loop breaks at the first offset in the range that is absent from `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not contiguous in general: log compaction, transaction control markers and deleted records all create gaps. If a gap sits at `last_committed + 1`, nothing past it is ever committed again, so the committed offset stops advancing and consumer lag grows without bound. After a restart, every message after the gap is reprocessed. The gap case should be treated as already complete, for example by skipping offsets that were never added, rather than as a blocker.

Queues are unbounded, so the claimed backpressure does not exist

Each per-queue `queue.Queue()` is created without a `maxsize`. Offsets are committed and the consumer keeps polling regardless of how far processing lags, so a slow downstream grows these queues without limit and memory use grows with it. The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring (around line 254) says the design provides 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', which is false for unbounded queues. Either bound the queues so `put` blocks, or fix the docstring and document the memory risk.

Racy assertion that total_items is nonzero right after submission

`test_stats_reporting` submits 10 items and then immediately asserts `stats["total_items"] > 0`. Worker threads may already have drained the queues by then, especially on a fast machine, so the test can fail intermittently. The assertion should be removed or the processing should be blocked until stats are checked.

Offset-gap test codifies the permanent-stall behaviour

`test_offset_gaps_block_commits` treats a never-seen offset (101) as a permanent blocker and asserts the commit stays at 100 until that offset arrives. This locks in the stall problem noted for `get_committable_offsets` and gives no coverage for gaps that will never be filled, such as compaction or transaction markers.

Graceful-shutdown test asserts almost nothing

`test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown` sends five results and then only asserts that `factory.queue_pool` is None. It does not wait for or check that the queued items were processed or that workers exited, so it would pass even if shutdown dropped in-flight work. Similarly, `test_thread_queue_parallel_concurrent_subscriptions` is named for concurrency but does not check any concurrent execution.

process_spans now uses ZADD on span-buf:s:* keys, and add-buffer.lua switched from SCARD/SUNIONSTORE to ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE. Any span-buf:s:* key written by the previous code is a Redis set, so ZADD, ZCARD and ZUNIONSTORE on it fail with WRONGTYPE, and _load_segment_data's ZSCAN fails as well. Segments buffered before the deploy (up to span_buffer_timeout / root timeout, and the queue entries still reference them) will error during processing and flushing. No key migration, dual-read, or key renaming is included.

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, zpopmin removes the lowest-scored (oldest) spans from the set. Those spans are dropped without any counter, log, or metric. Operators have no way to see that segments are being truncated.

When the same span payload is present in both the source and destination sets (for example, a redelivered Kafka message), its score is doubled, so its end_timestamp_precise no longer reflects the span's real end time. This distorts the eviction order introduced by this PR (zpopmin evicts by score) and any ordering that depends on it. An explicit AGGREGATE MIN or MAX should be used, or duplicates should be otherwise handled.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache short-circuits before the DB fallback, so a cached denial can keep hiding a newly granted permission

The denial cache is checked first in Check and returns deny immediately, before the cached-permission lookup and the DB fallback that this PR adds. A denial is written with a 30s TTL (shortCacheTTL) whenever the DB result is not allowed. If a user is checked on a resource before its permission row exists (for example, a dashboard or folder just created by that user, or a frontend poll), the denial is cached for 30s. Once the permission is written, every Check for that same user/action/name/folder returns false until the entry expires, which is the exact symptom this PR is meant to fix. The denial entry should be bypassed or invalidated when the permission is granted, or the check should go to the DB before trusting a denial. At minimum this trade-off needs to be documented and covered by a test.

Lark createEvent always uses the first destination calendar, so multi-host collective events are not created per host

Lark's createEvent, createAttendees, updateEvent and deleteEvent all take `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar` and ignore which credential is calling. CalendarManager calls each credential's createEvent with the full destination array. In a collective event with two hosts, every host's Lark credential therefore writes to host #1's calendar, and host #2's calendar gets no event. The same pattern applies to Office365 (createEvent, line 73 of that file) and CalDAV (createEvent filter in packages/lib/CalendarService.ts). The PR's stated goal of letting each host receive the event is not met for these integrations.

The destination externalId is attached to the result but never passed to the calendar services

createEvent now receives `externalId` and calls `calendar.createEvent(calEvent, credential.id)`, dropping the externalId. Only the Google service uses the credential to pick a calendar. Other services read event.destinationCalendar[0] or filter by it, so the per-destination externalId is lost. EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents (line 370) passes `destination.externalId` into createEvent, which is then discarded, so each destination entry results in the same write. The result's `externalId` field is also set from an argument that does nothing for these integrations, so the references stored for the booking will not match the calendars actually written to.

Team destination calendars are silently dropped when the organizer has no destination calendar

`evt.destinationCalendar` is set to `null` when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination calendar. The following line does `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)`, which is a no-op on null. For a collective event where the organizer has no destination but other hosts do, the other hosts' calendars are never used, which is the exact scenario this PR is meant to fix. The array should be initialised rather than optionally pushed to.

Team destination calendars can be duplicated and are collected inside a parallel map

teamDestinationCalendars is pushed inside `users.slice(1).map(async ...)`. The push happens before the await in each callback, so ordering is nondeterministic. Also, if multiple hosts share a destination calendar or an existing entry is already in evt.destinationCalendar, duplicates are not removed, so createAllCalendarEvents will write the same event more than once. Collecting the calendars synchronously after the users list is built, then de-duplicating by id, would avoid both problems.

Recurring cancellation deletes the same events once per calendar reference

The loop now iterates over every calendar reference. Inside the recurring branch, for each reference it maps over all user calendar credentials and deletes every updated booking's calendar event again. With two calendar references (the multi-host case this PR enables), each booking's event is deleted twice or more, and the duplicate deleteEvent calls push extra promises into apiDeletes. The recurring deletion should run once, outside the per-reference loop.

Office365 createEvent ignores the credential and writes every destination to the first calendar

createEvent reads `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = event.destinationCalendar ?? []` and uses that calendar's externalId for the URL. With multiple destinations, each per-destination createEvent call writes an event to the first calendar rather than the one belonging to its credential. This creates duplicate events on one account and none on the others.

No tests added for the multi-host collective behaviour being fixed

The PR adds a new multi-destination code path in EventManager, CalendarManager and the booking handlers, but the checklist says no tests were added and the testing section relies on manual Loom recordings. Given how many call sites changed from a single destination to an array, unit tests for EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents and updateAllCalendarEvents with multiple destinations would be needed to catch the regressions above.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Rejected import promises are unhandled and any uncaught access breaks silently

Because every entry is a promise created at module load, a failing import (missing dependency, syntax error in one app) produces an unhandled promise rejection when nobody has awaited that entry. Callers that index the store without `await` (any call site not updated in this PR) now receive a Promise, so `"lib" in app` is false and the code silently treats the app as not implemented, e.g. `getCalendar` logs a 'not implemented' warning and returns null.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments address the same concern: dynamic import failures are not handled gracefully. The golden comment recommends a try-catch around the await, while the candidate describes the resulting unhandled rejected promises and silent breakage; the wording differs but the underlying issue matches.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach drops calendar deletions for recurring cancellations

The `.forEach(async (credential) => {...})` callback pushes into `apiDeletes` only after `await getCalendar(...)` and the inner loop. Nothing awaits the callback promises, and `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs with the array as it was before the callbacks finished. As a result the calendar deletions are fire-and-forget: the handler reports success before they complete, and any rejection (e.g. from `deleteEvent`) becomes an unhandled rejection rather than an error surfaced to the caller. Use `for...of` with `await` or `Promise.all` over mapped promises, as the non-recurring branch already does.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying bug: async forEach callbacks are not awaited, so calendar deletions run fire-and-forget, can reject unhandled, and are not included in the awaited Promise.all. It also recommends the same fixes (for...of with await or Promise.all over mapped promises).

false_positives.candidate:
Object of import() promises starts loading every app eagerly

Each `import(...)` in the object literal is evaluated as soon as this module is loaded, so all ~30 app modules are fetched and evaluated on first import of `@calcom/app-store`, whether or not they are used. The PR title says 'async import', but this does not make loading lazy; it only changes the access pattern. A consumer that needs one app pays for all of them. Lazy loading would need a function per entry, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites updated to match.

getCalendarCredentials now yields promises in the `calendar` field while staying synchronous

`getCalendarCredentials` is still a synchronous function, so `getCalendar(credential)` returns a Promise that is stored as the `calendar` field. Any other caller of this exported function that uses `.calendar` as a Calendar object (not awaiting it) will break. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`. Other consumers of this exported API are not updated in the diff and should be checked, or the function should become async.

Async forEach makes the try/catch around calendar/video deletion ineffective

The `try { bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) } catch` block cannot catch errors from the async callbacks, since forEach does not return or await them. Previously `getCalendar` was synchronous and the try covered failures; now any error from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent` / `deleteMeeting` is an unhandled promise rejection and the reschedule flow continues without logging it. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` inside the try.

Same async forEach issue: calendar/video deletions are not awaited and errors are unhandled

The `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` callbacks are not awaited, so the deletion of the previous calendar event and video meeting runs in the background. The surrounding try/catch no longer catches anything. Rejections surface as unhandled promise rejections, and the caller cannot know whether the deletions succeeded.

Reschedule mutation fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting them

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` is not awaited, so the mutation returns before the old calendar event and video meeting are deleted. Failures become unhandled rejections. Rescheduling can therefore report success while the previous event stays on the calendar, or while errors go unreported. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

Unrelated blank-line change in getCalendarCredentials

A blank line is added before `return credentials.length ? ...` with no functional change. It adds noise to an already large async conversion.
